nameStory: Moss campion gets its name from its incredibly compact, cushion-like growth that looks just like a bright green moss from a distance. The 'campion' part comes from the old French word for 'champion,' referring to the plant's champion-like ability to survive in the harshest mountain conditions where few other flowers dare to grow.
description: Moss campion is a tiny but mighty wildflower that forms dense, rounded cushions barely a few inches tall but sometimes over a foot wide. This arctic and alpine specialist creates tight mats of needle-like evergreen leaves that feel springy underfoot, topped with brilliant pink five-petaled flowers in summer. It's like nature's own living pin cushion, perfectly designed to hug the ground and withstand fierce mountain winds and bitter cold.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms incredibly dense, rounded cushions that feel firm and springy when pressed, like a natural pillow made of tightly packed vegetation

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Tiny needle-like evergreen leaves packed so densely they create a solid green surface, feeling almost moss-like to the touch but stiffer

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright pink flowers with five notched petals sit directly on the cushion surface with no visible stems, creating a stunning contrast against the green mat

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Flowers often appear first on the south-facing side of the cushion, earning it the nickname 'compass plant'

habitat: In New England, moss campion is found only on the highest mountain peaks above treeline, particularly on exposed rocky slopes, cliff faces, and alpine meadows. Look for it on Mount Washington and other high peaks in the White Mountains, where it grows in thin, rocky soil that drains quickly and experiences extreme weather conditions.

seasonality.spring: The evergreen cushions emerge from melting snow looking bright green and compact, beginning to show flower buds as temperatures warm.
seasonality.summer: Brilliant pink flowers bloom from June through August, creating spectacular displays against the dense green cushions. This is the best time for identification and photography.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and cushions prepare for winter by tightening their growth even more, sometimes developing a slightly bronze tinge to the foliage.
seasonality.winter: The evergreen cushions remain visible above snow when possible, appearing as small green domes that can survive temperatures far below freezing.

funFact: Moss campion cushions can live for over 300 years and grow so slowly that a cushion the size of a dinner plate might be decades old - making these tiny alpine gardens some of the oldest living things you can find in New England's mountains!
confusionNotes: From a distance, moss campion looks exactly like a bright green moss until it blooms with those unmistakable pink flowers. Remember: if it's growing in a perfect dome shape above treeline and has pink flowers, it's moss campion - real mosses never produce such colorful blooms.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'moss' campion, this plant is actually more closely related to carnations and is completely unrelated to true mosses. The name reflects how it looks rather than what it actually is - a perfect example of how common names can be both helpful and misleading.
compareHints: Unlike its taller relatives like white campion or bladder campion that grow as upright herbs in lower elevations, moss campion has evolved this unique cushion form specifically for alpine survival. While other campions in the genus have visible stems and grow in meadows or roadsides, moss campion's stemless flowers and extreme dwarf habit make it instantly recognizable among the catchflies.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its catchfly relatives, white campion stands out for being densely fuzzy all over, while most other Silene species are smoother.
Among the catchflies and campions in New England, bladder campion is the only one with those distinctive inflated, balloon-like sepals - this feature alone separates it from all its relatives.
Among its catchfly relatives, ragged-robin is unique for its deeply divided petals - other Silene species like white campion and bladder campion have whole, uncut petals.
Among its catchfly relatives, rose campion is unmistakable due to its completely silver-woolly appearance and intense magenta flowers.
Red campion stands out from its Silene relatives by its bright pink color and preference for disturbed, rich soils.
Among its catchfly relatives, wild pink is distinguished by its extremely low, mat-forming growth habit and spring blooming time.
Among its catchfly relatives, sleepy catchfly stands out for having the smallest, least showy flowers that barely open.
Unlike its catchfly relatives that often have white or pale pink flowers, Maltese-cross blazes with intense scarlet-red blooms.
Among the catchflies and campions, starry campion stands out with its deeply fringed star-like petals and whorled leaf arrangement.
Among the red-flowered catchflies, royal catchfly stands out for its impressive height and late summer bloom time.
Among its catchfly relatives, night-flowering catchfly is unique for its extremely sticky, clammy texture and strict evening-flowering schedule.
Fire pink stands out dramatically from its catchfly relatives by its intense red color - most other Silene species have white, pink, or pale flowers.
Unlike white campion and bladder campion which have white flowers, sand catchfly's bright pink petals make it stand out.
Balkan catchfly is much smaller and more delicate than the common bladder campion, which has inflated balloon-like calyxes behind its flowers.
